title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about owning your development as a learner. You already know how university learning, assessment and feedback work. The step now is to take charge of them: to direct your own learning, judge your own work against the standard, and make feedback change what you do next.

By the end you will be able to direct your learning as a self-regulated process, apply marking criteria to appraise and raise your own work, and turn feedback into a cycle that feeds forward. These are the habits that mark out a self-regulating learner, and they carry straight into professional practice.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: direct your own learning as a self-regulated process of forethought, performance and evaluation
apply marking criteria to appraise your own work and raise its standard
turn feedback into a self-directed cycle that feeds forward into future work.

title: In real academic practice
body: Owning your development is what independent academic work rests on. Every project you plan and monitor, every draft you judge against the criteria before you submit it, every piece of feedback you act on rather than file away, is this ownership at work. The same self-regulation is what employers and research both expect of a graduate.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, directing your own learning: self-regulated learning as a process you drive. Second, setting your own standard: using marking criteria to appraise your own work. Third, making feedback feed forward: the feedback cycle run as a self-directed loop. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: Orientation
body: You know what learning at university involves. This lesson is about taking the wheel. Self-regulating learners do not wait to be told how to study; they set their own goals, watch how their approach is working, and change it when it is not. This lesson sets out that process so you can run it deliberately on your own work.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level the aim is not to learn that self-regulation exists, but to own it. You are expected to direct your own learning with little prompting, and to be able to say what you are doing and why. Treat the process here as something to apply to a real task you have in hand.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain self-regulated learning as taking control of your learning through forethought, performance and evaluation
analyse a worked example to distinguish a self-regulating learner from one who does not regulate
plan how you would regulate your own learning on a current task in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Self-regulated learning is the process of taking control of your own learning. Rather than working through whatever is set and hoping it goes well, you set your own goals, monitor how your approach is working as you go, and evaluate your performance afterwards so the next attempt is better. You drive it, not the tutor.

It runs in three phases. In forethought you plan: you set a goal and choose a strategy. In performance you act, and watch how the strategy is working. In evaluation you look back, judge the result against your goal, and decide what to change. The phases loop, so each evaluation feeds the next plan.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a task you have in hand now. What is your goal for it, how will you check your approach is working, and how will you judge the result afterwards?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Self-regulated learning means driving your own learning through three phases: forethought, where you set a goal and choose a strategy; performance, where you act and monitor; and evaluation, where you judge the result and decide what to change. You can now explain the process and see it at work in a learner's approach. The next lesson turns to one tool of self-regulation: judging your own work against the marking criteria.

title: Orientation
body: Marking criteria can look like something that happens to your work after you hand it in. This lesson turns that around. The criteria are the standard your work is judged against, and you can apply them yourself, before you submit, to see where your work stands and lift it. Owning the criteria is how you stop guessing what a good piece looks like.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to judge your own work, not only receive a judgement on it. The aim here is to read a set of marking criteria closely enough to apply them to a piece of work and justify the grade you would give, then to do the same for your own writing.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain how marking criteria define the standard your work is judged against
apply marking criteria to appraise a worked example and justify the judgement
use marking criteria to critique a piece of your own work in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Marking criteria are the measures a tutor uses to decide what mark your work earns. They are usually set out by level and by dimension: a dimension such as knowledge, communication or critical evaluation, described at each grade band so the difference between a pass and a first is spelled out. They are not secret, but published so you can use them too.

Applying them to your own work is self-assessment. You read your draft as a marker would, against each dimension, and ask honestly where it sits. Peer assessment is the same move made on each other's work. Both put the criteria in your hands, so you judge against the standard rather than hoping you have met it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Find the marking criteria for an assignment you are working on. Read your draft against each dimension. Which band does each meet, and what would move the weakest one up?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Marking criteria set out the standard your work is judged against, by dimension and by level. Applying them to your own draft is self-assessment: you read as a marker would, name the band each dimension meets, and revise where it falls short. You can now appraise a piece of work against criteria and justify the judgement. The next lesson does the same for the feedback you receive.

title: Orientation
body: Feedback is only worth the time it takes if it changes what you do next. This lesson treats feedback not as a verdict on finished work but as the start of a loop: something you review, make sense of, put into your own words, and apply to the next task. Run that way, feedback becomes the engine of your development.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to drive the feedback process yourself, not wait to be told what to fix. The aim here is to run the feedback cycle deliberately: to turn a tutor's comments into specific actions and carry them into your next piece of work, rather than reading them once and moving on.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: describe the feedback cycle (review, interpret, articulate, apply) as a self-directed loop
evaluate a worked example to judge how well a learner turned feedback into action
plan how you would feed feedback forward into your next piece of work in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
The feedback cycle is a way of using feedback so it actually improves your work. It has four stages. You review the feedback, reading it carefully and as a whole. You interpret it, working out what it really means and which comments matter most. You articulate it, putting the message into your own words as concrete actions. Then you apply it to your next piece of work.

What makes the cycle work is the mindset behind it. Treated as a final verdict, feedback stings and gets filed away. Treated as information to drive growth, the same comments become the most useful thing you receive. The cycle is self-directed: you run it, and it only closes when the next piece of work shows the change.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Take a recent piece of feedback. What did it really mean, and what is one concrete action it points to? Where will you apply that action next?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: The feedback cycle turns comments into improvement through four stages: review, interpret, articulate and apply. Run as a self-directed loop with a growth mindset, it closes only when your next piece of work shows the change. You can now describe the cycle, judge how well a learner used feedback, and plan how to feed your own feedback forward. Together with the earlier lessons, you now own the learning, assessment and feedback cycle.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Owning your development is no longer an idea but something you can do. You can direct your own learning as a self-regulated process of forethought, performance and evaluation. You can apply marking criteria to appraise your own work and raise its standard. And you can run feedback as a cycle that feeds forward into your next task. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, owning your development is something you practise in every module. Each task you plan and monitor, each draft you judge against the criteria, each piece of feedback you turn into action, is self-regulation at work. It is also what professional life rewards: the graduate who directs their own learning, judges their own work, and improves from feedback is the one who keeps growing.

title: Course Sources
instruction: This course draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 45 to 93 of Chapters 4 to 6 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026), covering self-regulated learning, assessment and feedback.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The three phases of self-regulated learning
body: The process runs in three phases that loop. Reveal each to see what it asks of you.
instruction: Select each phase to reveal it. Work through all three and the loop.

_items.title: Forethought: plan before you start
_items.body: You set a specific goal for the task and choose a strategy to reach it. A self-regulating learner decides in advance what a good result would look like and how to get there, rather than starting and seeing what happens.

_items.title: Performance: act and monitor
_items.body: You carry out the work and watch how the strategy is doing as you go. Because you are tracking progress against the goal you set, you notice early when something is not working and can change course.

_items.title: Evaluation: judge and adjust
_items.body: You weigh the result against your goal. What worked, what did not, and why? Evaluation is honest reflection with a purpose: deciding what to keep and what to change next time.

_items.title: The loop closes
_items.body: Evaluation is not the end. What you learn about your own approach feeds straight into the forethought of your next task, so each cycle of work makes the next one sharper.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Three dimensions of the standard
body: Marking criteria usually judge your work along a few dimensions. Read each card to see what one asks of you.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Knowledge and understanding
_items.subtitle: Do you know it?
_items.text: Does the work show accurate, relevant knowledge of the topic, and real understanding rather than repetition? At the top band it is selective and well judged, not everything you found.

_items.title: Communication
_items.subtitle: Is it clear?
_items.text: Is the work structured, readable and properly referenced, so the argument is easy to follow? Clear communication is marked, not assumed: a strong point made badly loses credit.

_items.title: Critical evaluation
_items.subtitle: Do you weigh it?
_items.text: Does the work weigh evidence and argument rather than just describe them? This dimension usually separates the higher bands: it rewards judgement, not coverage.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The four stages of the feedback cycle
body: The feedback cycle turns comments into action in four stages. Reveal each to see what it asks of you.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Review
_items.body: Read the whole of the feedback, not just the mark. Resist the urge to react. The aim at this stage is to take in everything that was said, including what went well, before you decide what to do about it.

_items.title: Interpret
_items.body: Work out what the feedback actually means and which comments matter most. A remark like 'needs more critical depth' has to be decoded into something specific. Interpreting well is where most of the value is won or lost.

_items.title: Articulate
_items.body: Put the message into your own words as concrete actions. 'Weigh the evidence before stating a conclusion' is an action; 'be more critical' is not. Articulating turns a comment into something you can actually do.

_items.title: Apply
_items.body: Carry the actions into your next piece of work. This is the stage that closes the loop: feedback has changed nothing until the next task shows it. Applying is what turns a comment into development.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students have four weeks to write the same essay.

{{learner-a}} starts reading straight away and writes as the material accumulates, with no goal beyond finishing and no check on whether the approach is working, until the essay comes back with a disappointing mark. {{learner-a}} was busy throughout, but never stood back to monitor or adjust. This is working without regulating.

{{learner-b}} begins by setting a goal: a clear argument supported by evidence, finished a week early. {{learner-b}} chooses a strategy, then checks at the halfway point whether the argument is holding together, and changes tack when one section will not work. Afterwards {{learner-b}} notes what to do differently next time. This is self-regulated learning: forethought, performance and evaluation, run on purpose.

Both students worked hard. Only {{learner-b}} drove the process, and it is {{learner-b}} who will improve from one essay to the next.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students apply the same marking criteria to their own draft before submitting.

{{learner-a}} reads the draft through, feels it is fine, and submits. Asked which band it meets on critical evaluation, {{learner-a}} cannot say: the draft describes the sources well but does not weigh them. {{learner-a}} judged the work by effort and length, not against the criteria, and so missed that it sat a band lower than hoped.

{{learner-b}} reads the draft against each dimension in turn. Knowledge: strong. Communication: clear, though one section wanders. Critical evaluation: thin, mostly description. {{learner-b}} can name the band each dimension meets and why, and uses that to revise the weak section before submitting. The judgement is reasoned and tied to the criteria.

Both had the same criteria. Only {{learner-b}} applied them, and turned the appraisal into a better piece of work.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students receive the same comment on an essay: their argument describes the sources but does not evaluate them.

{{learner-a}} reads the comment, feels the mark is harsh, and files the essay away. On the next assignment the same comment comes back. {{learner-a}} reviewed the feedback but never interpreted it into an action or applied it, so nothing changed. The feedback was received, not used.

{{learner-b}} reads the comment, works out what evaluating would actually look like, and writes it as a concrete action: weigh each source's evidence before using it. On the next essay {{learner-b}} does exactly that, and the comment does not return. The cycle has closed: review, interpret, articulate, apply.

Both were given the same feedback. Only {{learner-b}} fed it forward, and only {{learner-b}}'s work improved because of it.

title: Regulating a task
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these habits to turn self-regulation into something you do on a real task.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I set a specific goal for this task, not just a plan to finish it?
Have I chosen a strategy, and can I say why it fits this task?
Have I set a point to check whether the strategy is working?
Did I notice when something was not working, and change it?
Have I judged the result against the goal I set, not just the mark?
Have I decided one thing to do differently on the next task?

title: Appraising your own work
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these checks to apply marking criteria to your own draft before you submit it.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I found the actual marking criteria for this assignment?
Have I read my draft against each dimension separately?
Can I name the band each dimension meets, and say why?
Have I been honest where the work is weaker than I hoped?
Have I used the appraisal to change the draft, not just rate it?
Could I justify my judgement to a tutor or peer?

title: Running the feedback cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these steps to run the feedback cycle on a real piece of feedback.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I read all the feedback, including what went well, before reacting?
Have I worked out what each important comment actually means?
Have I turned the main comments into specific actions?
Have I written the actions somewhere I will see them next time?
Have I applied them to my next piece of work?
Did the same comment stop coming back?

title: Formative check: what self-regulated learning is
displayTitle: Which statement best captures what self-regulated learning means?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement best captures what self-regulated learning means?

_items.text: Taking control of your own learning by setting goals, monitoring your approach, and evaluating your performance.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is self-regulated learning: you drive the goals, the monitoring and the evaluation.

_items.text: Working steadily through everything your tutors set you.
_items.feedback: Working through what is set is not the same as regulating it, with no goal-setting, monitoring or evaluation of your own.

_items.text: Studying alone, without help from tutors or peers.
_items.feedback: Self-regulation is about driving your learning, not working in isolation; you can regulate and still seek help.

_items.text: Being naturally good at a subject so you need less effort.
_items.feedback: Self-regulated learning is a process you run, not a matter of natural ability.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Self-regulated learning is driving your own learning through goals, monitoring and evaluation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where you set the goals, monitor and evaluate your own learning.
_incorrect.final: Self-regulated learning means taking control through forethought, performance and evaluation. Working through set tasks, studying alone, or natural ability are not it.

title: Formative check: spotting self-regulation
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second learner self-regulating rather than simply hard-working?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second learner self-regulating rather than simply hard-working?

_items.text: They set a goal, monitored whether their strategy was working, and adjusted it along the way.
_items.feedback: Yes. Setting a goal, monitoring and adjusting is self-regulation in action.

_items.text: They spent more hours on the essay than the first learner.
_items.feedback: Both learners worked hard; hours are not what made the difference.

_items.text: They started their reading earlier than the first learner.
_items.feedback: Starting earlier helps, but it is not what makes the process self-regulated.

_items.text: They asked the tutor for more guidance before starting.
_items.feedback: The second learner drove the process themselves rather than relying on extra guidance.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second learner set a goal, monitored their strategy and adjusted it, which is self-regulation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second learner DID with the process, beyond working hard.
_incorrect.final: The second learner was self-regulating because they set a goal, monitored their strategy and adjusted it. Extra hours, an earlier start or more guidance are not the point.

title: Formative check: planning your own regulation
displayTitle: You are planning a current task in {{context}}. Which move best shows the forethought phase of self-regulation?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move best shows the forethought phase of self-regulation?

_items.text: Setting a specific goal for the task and choosing a strategy to reach it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Forethought in {{context}} means setting a goal and choosing a strategy before you begin.

_items.text: Starting the work and seeing how it goes.
_items.feedback: Starting without a goal or strategy skips the forethought phase.

_items.text: Waiting for the tutor to explain exactly what to do.
_items.feedback: Waiting to be told is the opposite of driving your own learning.

_items.text: Comparing your mark with other students once it is returned.
_items.feedback: That comes after the work and is not forethought.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, forethought means setting a goal and choosing a strategy before you start.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Forethought happens before the work: look for setting a goal and a strategy.
_incorrect.final: Forethought in {{context}} means setting a specific goal and choosing a strategy before you begin. The other options skip or follow that phase.

title: Formative check: what marking criteria are
displayTitle: What are marking criteria, and what are they for?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What are marking criteria, and what are they for?

_items.text: The measures, set out by dimension and level, that define the standard your work is judged against.
_items.feedback: Yes. Criteria define the standard, by dimension and level, and are published so you can use them.

_items.text: A private checklist tutors keep so students cannot predict their marks.
_items.feedback: Criteria are published, not secret; they are meant to be used by students too.

_items.text: The total number of sources a piece of work is expected to cite.
_items.feedback: A source count is not the standard; criteria describe the quality expected across dimensions.

_items.text: A fixed word count that work must reach to pass.
_items.feedback: Word count is not the standard; criteria describe the quality of the work.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Marking criteria define the standard, by dimension and level, and are published for you to use.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about the standard your work is judged against, by dimension and level.
_incorrect.final: Marking criteria are the measures that define the standard, by dimension and level. They are not a secret checklist, a source count or a word count.

title: Formative check: justifying a judgement
displayTitle: In the worked example, what let the second learner justify the grade their draft would earn?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What let the second learner justify the grade their draft would earn?

_items.text: They appraised the draft against each dimension of the criteria and could say which band it met and why.
_items.feedback: Yes. Judging each dimension against the criteria is what makes the judgement justifiable.

_items.text: They wrote more than the first learner.
_items.feedback: Length is not what justifies a grade; appraising against the criteria is.

_items.text: They submitted the draft earlier than the first learner.
_items.feedback: Timing does not justify a judgement about quality.

_items.text: They preferred their own work to the first learner's.
_items.feedback: Preference is not a reasoned judgement against the criteria.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second learner judged each dimension against the criteria, so the grade was justified.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for how the second learner tied the judgement to the criteria.
_incorrect.final: The second learner could justify the grade because they appraised the draft against each dimension and named the band it met. Length, timing or preference do not justify a judgement.

title: Formative check: critiquing your own work
displayTitle: You are about to submit a piece of work in {{context}}. How do you use the marking criteria to critique it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How do you use the marking criteria to critique your own work?

_items.text: Read the work against each dimension, decide the band it meets, and revise where it falls short.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, that is applying the criteria to appraise and raise your own work.

_items.text: Check it is long enough and has enough references, then submit.
_items.feedback: Length and reference count are not the standard the criteria set.

_items.text: Submit it and wait to see which band the marker gives it.
_items.feedback: That leaves the judgement entirely to the marker rather than critiquing it yourself.

_items.text: Compare it with a friend's work and match their length.
_items.feedback: Matching a friend's length is not judging against the criteria.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, you read the work against each dimension, decide the band, and revise where it falls short.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that applies the criteria dimension by dimension and revises.
_incorrect.final: Critiquing your own work in {{context}} means reading it against each dimension, deciding the band, and revising where it falls short. The others skip the criteria.

title: Formative check: the feedback cycle
displayTitle: Which of these best describes the feedback cycle?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these best describes the feedback cycle?

_items.text: Reviewing, interpreting, articulating and applying feedback as a self-directed loop that closes on your next piece of work.
_items.feedback: Yes. Those four stages, run as a loop, are the feedback cycle.

_items.text: Reading the mark and comments once when work is returned.
_items.feedback: Reading once is only the start; the cycle interprets, articulates and applies.

_items.text: Asking the tutor to re-mark work you disagree with.
_items.feedback: Challenging a mark is not the feedback cycle.

_items.text: Keeping every piece of feedback filed in case you need it.
_items.feedback: Filing feedback is not using it; the cycle applies it to the next task.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The feedback cycle is review, interpret, articulate and apply, run as a self-directed loop.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option with all four stages run as a loop.
_incorrect.final: The feedback cycle is reviewing, interpreting, articulating and applying feedback as a loop. Reading once, challenging a mark or filing it are not the cycle.

title: Formative check: turning feedback into action
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the second learner's work improve when the first learner's did not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the second learner's work improve when the first learner's did not?

_items.text: They interpreted the comment into a concrete action and applied it to the next piece of work.
_items.feedback: Yes. Interpreting and applying is what closed the loop and improved the work.

_items.text: They disagreed with the mark more strongly.
_items.feedback: Disagreeing with a mark does not improve the next piece of work.

_items.text: They received more detailed feedback than the first learner.
_items.feedback: Both received the same comment; the difference was what they did with it.

_items.text: They kept the feedback filed for later reference.
_items.feedback: Filing feedback is what the first learner did; it changed nothing.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second learner interpreted the comment into an action and applied it, so the work improved.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second learner DID with the same comment.
_incorrect.final: The second learner's work improved because they interpreted the comment into a concrete action and applied it. The same feedback, filed or merely disputed, changed nothing.

title: Formative check: feeding feedback forward
displayTitle: You have feedback on a piece of work in {{context}}. Which move best feeds it forward into your next task?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move best feeds feedback forward into your next task?

_items.text: Turn the main comments into specific actions and apply them to your next piece of work.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, turning comments into actions and applying them is how feedback feeds forward.

_items.text: Read the comments once, then focus on the mark.
_items.feedback: Reading once and focusing on the mark does not change your next task.

_items.text: File the feedback and move on to the next deadline.
_items.feedback: Filing feedback leaves the cycle open; nothing is applied.

_items.text: Decide the feedback was unfair and set it aside.
_items.feedback: Setting feedback aside means it feeds nothing forward.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, you turn the main comments into specific actions and apply them next time.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that turns comments into actions and applies them.
_incorrect.final: Feeding feedback forward in {{context}} means turning the main comments into specific actions and applying them to your next piece of work. The others leave the loop open.

body: Self-regulated learning is best described as...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How is self-regulated learning best described?

_items.text: taking control of your own learning by setting goals, monitoring your approach and evaluating your performance.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is self-regulated learning.

_items.text: working steadily through whatever your tutors set.
_items.feedback: Working through set tasks is not regulating your own learning.

_items.text: studying without any help from tutors or peers.
_items.feedback: Self-regulation is not the same as working in isolation.

_items.text: having enough natural ability to need little effort.
_items.feedback: It is a process you run, not natural ability.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Self-regulated learning is taking control through goals, monitoring and evaluation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about who drives the goals, the monitoring and the evaluation.

body: Which of these is the forethought phase of self-regulated learning?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is the forethought phase of self-regulated learning?

_items.text: Setting a goal for a task and choosing a strategy before you begin.
_items.feedback: Yes. Forethought happens before the work.

_items.text: Judging the finished work against your goal.
_items.feedback: That is evaluation, which comes after.

_items.text: Comparing your mark with other students'.
_items.feedback: That follows the work and is not forethought.

_items.text: Carrying out the work as planned.
_items.feedback: That is the performance phase.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Forethought is setting a goal and choosing a strategy before you start.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which phase happens before the work begins?

body: What is the main purpose of marking criteria for a self-regulating student?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the main purpose of marking criteria for a self-regulating student?

_items.text: To appraise their own work against the standard before they submit it.
_items.feedback: Yes. You apply the criteria to your own work.

_items.text: To find out the minimum word count required.
_items.feedback: Criteria describe quality, not word count.

_items.text: To see how many sources they must cite.
_items.feedback: A source count is not the standard.

_items.text: To predict the mark without reading the work.
_items.feedback: Criteria are applied by reading the work against them.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A self-regulating student uses criteria to appraise their own work against the standard.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What does a self-regulating student DO with the criteria?

body: Applying marking criteria to your own draft, dimension by dimension, is...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Applying marking criteria to your own draft, dimension by dimension, is...

_items.text: self-assessment.
_items.feedback: Yes. Judging your own work against the criteria is self-assessment.

_items.text: proofreading.
_items.feedback: Proofreading checks surface errors, not the standard.

_items.text: plagiarism.
_items.feedback: That is unrelated; self-assessment is judging your own work.

_items.text: summarising.
_items.feedback: Summarising condenses content; it does not judge against criteria.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Judging your own work against the criteria is self-assessment.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What do we call judging your own work against the criteria?

body: The four stages of the feedback cycle are...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What are the four stages of the feedback cycle?

_items.text: review, interpret, articulate and apply.
_items.feedback: Yes. Those are the four stages.

_items.text: read, mark, file and forget.
_items.feedback: That is the opposite of using feedback.

_items.text: submit, wait, receive and store.
_items.feedback: Those describe receiving feedback, not using it.

_items.text: plan, draft, edit and submit.
_items.feedback: Those are stages of writing, not the feedback cycle.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The feedback cycle is review, interpret, articulate and apply.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Recall the four named stages of the cycle.

body: Feedback has genuinely fed forward when...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: When has feedback genuinely fed forward?

_items.text: you have applied it to your next piece of work and the issue no longer recurs.
_items.feedback: Yes. The loop closes when the next task shows the change.

_items.text: you have read every comment carefully.
_items.feedback: Reading is only the first stage.

_items.text: you have filed it for future reference.
_items.feedback: Filing it changes nothing.

_items.text: you have accepted that the mark was fair.
_items.feedback: Accepting the mark does not change your next task.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Feedback feeds forward only when you apply it and the issue stops recurring.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. When does feedback actually change your next piece of work?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: directing your own learning, judging your work against the marking criteria, and feeding feedback forward. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage the aim is to see these three as one self-regulated loop, rather than three separate skills. Run together across each piece of work, they are how you own your development as an independent student.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: bring together directing your learning, judging your work against the criteria, and feeding feedback forward as one loop
recognise the three strands working together in a student's ongoing work
plan how you will keep running this one practice across your {{context}} study

title: Concept: definition
body: Owning your development is self-regulation made whole. It is one loop you run again and again: you set a goal and drive the work, you judge the result against the criteria, and you feed what you learn, including feedback, into the next piece. The three ideas from the earlier lessons are the parts of that single loop.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, owning your development means running one loop across every piece of work, in any subject. You set a goal and drive the task, judge the result against the criteria, and feed what you learn, including feedback, into the next piece. Across a module, those connected rounds are what steady improvement rests on.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of one piece of work you have coming up this term. How will you set its goal, judge the draft against the criteria, and feed your last piece of feedback into it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Owning your development is the three strands run as one loop: direct the work, judge it against the criteria, and feed feedback forward into the next piece. You can now recognise that one practice at work and plan to keep it going. It is the loop, repeated, not any single task, that raises how you study.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: Self-regulation is one loop you run again and again, not four separate tasks. Select each part of the cycle to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Set a goal
_items.body: Set a goal for the work and plan how you will approach it.

_items.title: Drive the work
_items.body: Drive the work, checking as you go whether it is building towards that goal.

_items.title: Judge the piece
_items.body: Judge the finished piece against the marking criteria, dimension by dimension.

_items.title: Carry forward
_items.body: Turn the feedback and your own appraisal into one change you carry into the next piece, then set the next goal. The loop turns again.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students finish a module having set out with the same goal and the same early feedback. One treats each assignment as a fresh start, never checking the work against the criteria or acting on what was said before. The other sets a goal, judges each draft against the criteria, and carries one piece of feedback forward each time. Over the term the second student's work improves, because the three strands ran as one practice.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to keep the practice going
body: Use these to keep the three strands running as one loop, rather than treating each piece of work as a fresh start.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I set a clear goal before starting, not just begin working?
Did I check part-way whether the work was building towards that goal?
Did I judge the finished work against the criteria, not just my effort?
Did I read any feedback for what it points to, not just the mark?
Did I carry one change forward into my next piece of work?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to run the three strands as one loop rather than three separate skills?
body: Why is it more useful to run the three strands as one loop rather than three separate skills?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to run the three strands as one loop rather than three separate skills?

_items.text: Because each strand feeds the next: your goal shapes the work, the criteria judge it, and the feedback changes your next goal.
_items.feedback: Yes. Run as one loop, each strand feeds the next, so the work improves over time.

_items.text: Because doing all three at once means you never have to judge your own work.
_items.feedback: Owning your development includes judging your own work honestly. That is the point of it.

_items.text: Because running them separately, once each, is enough to fix how you study for good.
_items.feedback: A single pass rarely changes a habit. The loop works when you repeat it.

_items.text: Because one loop takes less thought than directing, judging and using feedback on their own.
_items.feedback: It is not about less thought. One loop joins the three up so the thinking pays off.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Run as one loop, each strand feeds the next, so your work improves across your studies.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you gain by joining the three strands into one repeated loop.

displayTitle: A student sets a goal for an essay, drives the work, judges the draft against the criteria, acts on earlier feedback, and the finished essay is stronger. What does this show?
body: A student sets a goal for an essay, drives the work, judges the draft against the criteria, acts on earlier feedback, and the finished essay is stronger. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student sets a goal for an essay, drives the work, judges the draft against the criteria, acts on earlier feedback, and the finished essay is stronger. What does this show?

_items.text: That the three strands work as one practice: directing, judging and feeding feedback forward together produced a stronger piece.
_items.feedback: Yes. The whole loop ran, and the work improved because of it.

_items.text: That the first essay was marked too generously.
_items.feedback: The point is not the mark. It is that the three strands together improved the work.

_items.text: That only students who already do well can use the three strands.
_items.feedback: The practice helped this student improve, whatever their starting point.

_items.text: That acting on feedback alone, without a goal or the criteria, is what improved the essay.
_items.feedback: Feedback was one strand. The gain came from running all three together.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Directing, judging and feeding feedback forward ran as one loop, and the work improved.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how many strands the student used together, and what improved as a result.

displayTitle: You want to use this one practice to improve how you study {{context}} this term. Which plan best runs the three strands as one loop?
body: You want to use this one practice to improve how you study {{context}} this term. Which plan best runs the three strands as one loop?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this one practice to improve how you study your subject this term. Which plan best runs the three strands as one loop?

_items.text: On each piece of work, set a goal, drive it, judge it against the criteria, act on feedback, and carry one change into the next.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs all three strands as one loop, again and again.

_items.text: Direct your learning now, and leave judging your work and using feedback until final year.
_items.feedback: The strands work together, not years apart. Run them as one loop on each piece.

_items.text: Judge your work against the criteria only, and ignore your goals and any feedback.
_items.feedback: That is one strand on its own. The practice joins all three.

_items.text: Wait for your tutor to set the goal, mark the work, and tell you what to change.
_items.feedback: Owning your development means you drive the loop, not wait to be driven.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Setting a goal, judging against the criteria, and feeding feedback forward on each piece keeps all three strands running as one loop.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan runs all three strands together, over and over.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Owning your development, as this course uses it, is best described as:
body: Owning your development, as this course uses it, is best described as:
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Owning your development, as this course uses it, is best described as:

_items.text: Running directing your learning, judging your work against the criteria, and feeding feedback forward together as one loop.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three strands form one self-directed practice.

_items.text: Choosing whichever one of the three strands suits a task and ignoring the rest.
_items.feedback: The practice runs all three together, not one at a time.

_items.text: Waiting for tutors to set goals, mark your work, and tell you what to change.
_items.feedback: Owning your development means you drive the loop yourself.

_items.text: Doing more work than other students on every task.
_items.feedback: Effort alone is not the practice. The loop is what matters.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student plans an assignment, checks their draft against the criteria, acts on last term's feedback, and improves on the previous piece. Which strands are at work?
body: A student plans an assignment, checks their draft against the criteria, acts on last term's feedback, and improves on the previous piece. Which strands are at work?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student plans an assignment, checks their draft against the criteria, acts on last term's feedback, and improves on the previous piece. Which strands are at work?

_items.text: All three, run together as one practice: directing, judging against the criteria, and feeding feedback forward.
_items.feedback: Yes. The whole loop is at work.

_items.text: Only feeding feedback forward, since the mark improved.
_items.feedback: Acting on feedback was one strand. The student also set a goal and judged the work.

_items.text: Only judging against the criteria, since a draft was checked.
_items.feedback: Checking the draft was one strand. Planning and feedback were at work too.

_items.text: None; the improvement was simply luck.
_items.feedback: The improvement came from running the three strands together, not from luck.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
